summary:
Apurímac stands under the national framework of Peru. No Apurímac-specific trans statute, ordinance or enforcement finding appears in the sources attached to this record, so the rules a visitor faces in the department are Peru's national laws and the national patterns of their application.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities. Bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, were merged and approved unanimously by the congressional Women and Family Commission on 20 February 2025. The measure bars trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their sex at birth, with exceptions only for custody, situations requiring medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and it bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The bill followed a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for the narrow listed exceptions. The Inter-American institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, holds that this directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents, which contains the bathroom mandate and also bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity', applies throughout Peru including Apurímac.

LGBTI activist Gianna Camacho, cited on the commission's February 2025 approval, warns that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, and states that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The restriction reaches private as well as public life: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people in Peru is documented and rising. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases over 2020–2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints recorded in 2020 alone.

One case marks the limits and the possibility of protection. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code. Congress voted in 2017 to strip the protections from the new code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Speech and association are constrained by the same legislative package. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. Two protective developments are on record: in June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
tangentialFactors:
Peru's position is unusual in its subregion. The 2017 repeal left it one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, with no LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, while the Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity is protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The bathroom provision therefore sits against an inter-American standard it does not meet, a tension IDEHPUCP makes explicit by anchoring its objection in article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights.

Discrimination under the policy is enforced beyond state facilities. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's complaint against a gym applying the restriction, and on-air harassment of Susel Paredes by presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV carried the 'men's room' formulation into national broadcasting. Official hostility is also on the record inside the legislature itself: IDEHPUCP documented dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Enforcement figures are acknowledged to understate the problem. Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender and co-author of the 2024 report, stresses that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The 170 recorded rights-violation cases over 2020–2023 include state violence, so exposure is not limited to private actors.

Human Rights Watch states that the child-protection framing of the April 2025 law is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people, with vague articles and an article 4 media ban enabling censorship of identity, artistic and educational material and the obscenity minimum raised from three to four years. Set against that, an Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional in July 2025 after an activist legal challenge, and June 2024 health guidance dropped pathologising terminology for gender diversity, a change described as advancing dignity for trans patients.
localsOnly:
Residents of Apurímac live under the same national codes as visitors, but the burdens of enforcement fall on those who must use public services daily. Article 5 of the April 2025 law applies to any public sanitary service, so routine access for trans residents depends on the exceptions listed in the merged bills and, as Gianna Camacho warns, on the personal judgment of security staff, including demands for identity documents. The absence of any record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms undercuts the rationale offered for the restriction.

Trans residents carry the greatest share of recorded lethal violence. Of 54 TLGBI murders over 2020–2023, 30 victims were trans women; killings rose to 19 in 2023 with 12 trans women killed. The 170 recorded rights-violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints in 2020 alone, and the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI data are treated by their co-author as a sub-registry rather than a full count.

The February 2023 killing of Rubí Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans sex worker abducted by a gang in central Lima and shot about 30 times in Carabayllo as part of an extortion scheme, illustrates the specific exposure of sex workers. Since 2017 trans and LGBT people have had no hate-crime or anti-discrimination coverage in the Penal Code after Congress stripped the provisions with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress votes, following an April Constitutional Committee decision and a petition claiming one million signatures.

Two changes benefit residents directly. From June 2024 official health guidance no longer uses pathologising terminology for gender diversity, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court struck down an anti-equality decree after an activist challenge. The December 2025 sentence of 17 years against Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, nearly 20 years after the attack, is Peru's first conviction motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.
outOfScopeNotes:
The record contains no Apurímac-specific source. Nothing in the inventory documents a departmental ordinance, a local enforcement pattern, an incident in Apurímac, or local facility provision; whether any prefecture or municipal authority in the department has issued guidance implementing the April 2025 restroom rule is unresolved and not sourced here.

The legislative sequence is not fully reconciled in the sources. Infobae reports committee approval of the merged bills 6506 and 8457 on 20 February 2025, while IDEHPUCP reports plenary approval and exemption from a second vote on 2 April 2025; whether these are the same instrument at successive stages, and whether the final text has been promulgated and is in force in Apurímac, is not stated and remains unresolved.

The violence totals are national and are not disaggregated by region. Whether any of the 54 murders or 170 rights-violation cases recorded over 2020–2023 occurred in Apurímac is not sourced; the co-author of the report describes the figures as a sub-registry, so absence of departmental cases cannot be read as absence of incidents.

Disposal of the gym complaint by the consumer-protection body is recorded without its legal basis or any appeal outcome, so whether that dismissal is final is unresolved. The Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 and the July 2025 Lima ruling against an anti-equality decree are noted as counterweights, but the sources do not establish how either has been applied against the April 2025 bathroom provision.
